slides.text: A constant needs its value at compile time, so it cannot call a normal function. A `const fn` is a function the compiler is allowed to run while it builds the program.
A `const fn` is still a normal function: call it with any value at run time too. The only difference is the word `const` in front, and a body that the compiler can run.

What fits in the body of a `const fn`:

- arithmetic, `let` and `let mut`
- `if`, `match` and `while`
- calls to other `const fn`

No `for` loops and no printing. A constant that overflows stops the build, not the run.

notes.text: Lets a constant call this function.

exercises.title: Why only one const?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the reason `double` is a `const fn` and `triple` is not.
options: `double` gets a literal and `triple` a variable
A `const fn` runs faster than a normal one
`LIMIT` calls `double`, so it must be a `const fn`
exercises.explanation: A constant is computed at compile time, so it may only call a `const fn`. `triple` is only called at run time, where a normal function is fine.

slides.text:
The body of a `const fn` can decide and repeat, as long as the compiler can follow it: `if`, `match` and `while` all work, and so does a function calling itself.

This session builds three of them.

exercises.title: Plan prices
exercises.guide: A `match` inside a `const fn` picks the price of a plan while compiling.

chunks.text:
fn main() {
}

chunks.guide: Tier 1 costs 10, tier 2 costs 8, and any other tier costs 5.
Two constants, each computed by a call.
chunks.text:
const STARTER: u32 = rate(1);
const FALLBACK: u32 = rate(7);

println!("tier 1: {} a month", STARTER);
    println!("tier 7: {} a month", FALLBACK);

output.text:
tier 1: 10 a month
tier 7: 5 a month

exercises.title: A power of two
exercises.guide: Repeat the multiplication while steps are left, then give back the product.

exercises.title: Why a while loop?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick why it uses `while` and not `for`.
options: A `for` loop runs slower inside a constant
A `for` needs iterators, which it cannot run
A `const fn` may only loop a fixed number of times
A `for` loop cannot change a `let mut` variable
exercises.explanation: `for` relies on iterators, which the compiler cannot run yet. Variables and `+=` are fine in a `const fn`, and `while` does the same job.

exercises.title: Ways to seat guests
exercises.guide: A `const fn` can call itself. Its result can fill a constant and a static.

chunks.text:
fn main() {
}

chunks.guide: Multiply `n` by the factorial of the number below it. It stops at 1.
One constant and one static, both filled by calls.

notes.text: A static also needs a value known at compile time.

chunks.text:
const FIVE_GUESTS: u32 = factorial(5);
static FOUR_GUESTS: u32 = factorial(4);

chunks.guide: Print how many seatings each has.
chunks.text:
println!("5 guests: {} seatings", FIVE_GUESTS);
    println!("4 guests: {} seatings", FOUR_GUESTS);

exercises.title: When does it overflow?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick what happens on `cargo run`.
options: 100, then a panic at run time
The build stops, nothing is printed
exercises.explanation: The compiler computes every constant while building, used or not. `square(20)` is 400, which does not fit in a `u8`, so the overflow stops the build.
